q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE difference between direct and indirect imperial rule in the period c. 1750 to c. 1900.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why the British preferred indirect rule in parts of Africa, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which both direct and indirect rule disrupted indigenous political structures.

sample_answers.a: Under direct rule, European officials replaced indigenous authorities and imposed European laws and administration; under indirect rule, Europeans governed through existing chiefs and kings, who kept their titles but answered to colonial overseers.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, indirect rule was far cheaper: Britain could control vast territories with a handful of European officers by using native authorities to collect taxes and keep order, avoiding the cost of a large colonial bureaucracy.
sample_answers.c: Even under indirect rule, chiefs who had once answered to their own people became agents of the colonial state, enforcing taxes and labor demands; this corrupted their legitimacy and turned traditional authority into an instrument of foreign domination.

q1.stimulus:
Historians distinguish between two main methods of European colonial administration in the nineteenth century. In direct rule, practiced most fully by the French, European officials displaced indigenous rulers and attempted to remake colonial societies on the European model, imposing European law, language, and bureaucracy. In indirect rule, developed most systematically by the British in Africa, Europeans governed through existing kings and chiefs, who retained their positions but took orders from colonial officers. Indirect rule was attractive because it was cheap — a few dozen British officials could control millions of people — and because it reduced the risk of rebellion by preserving the appearance of traditional authority. Yet historians stress that indirect rule was not truly traditional: chiefs became salaried agents of empire, and colonial demands for taxes and labor transformed the societies they supposedly preserved.
—Historian's account of imperial administration in the period c. 1750–1900

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE principle Lugard advocates for governing colonized peoples.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which indirect rule, as described by Lugard, differed from direct administration by Europeans.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why indirect rule could create tensions between colonial chiefs and their own peoples.

sample_answers.a: Lugard advocates ruling through native chiefs and institutions rather than replacing them, arguing that Europeans should guide and supervise indigenous authorities instead of administering directly.
sample_answers.b: Under indirect rule, African chiefs continued to hold courts, collect taxes, and maintain order under British oversight, whereas direct administration would have installed European officers in every post and swept away native institutions.
sample_answers.c: Chiefs became responsible for enforcing unpopular colonial demands — taxes, forced labor, cash-crop quotas — so their people increasingly saw them as collaborators with foreign rulers rather than as legitimate traditional leaders.

q2.stimulus:
The British policy of indirect administration through the native chiefs has been proved to be the most economical and efficient. The native ruler, however corrupt or inefficient, is the instrument through which the British officer must work. To depose him and set up a European in his place would be to destroy the whole fabric of native society. Our task is to educate the native ruler in the principles of just government, to assist him with advice, and to support his authority — while ensuring that his administration serves the interests of both the British Empire and his own people.
—Adapted from Frederick Lugard, The Dual Mandate in British Tropical Africa, 1922

q3.directions: Use the map below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE pattern shown on the map regarding European control of Africa in 1914.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the rapid European partition of Africa between 1880 and 1914.
parts.c: Explain ONE difference between British and French colonial holdings as shown on the map.

sample_answers.a: By 1914 nearly the entire African continent is divided among European powers, with only Ethiopia and Liberia remaining independent — showing how completely Africa was partitioned within a single generation.
sample_answers.b: Industrial rivalries, the search for raw materials and markets, and nationalist competition (especially after the Berlin Conference of 1884–85 set rules for claiming territory) drove European powers to seize African colonies before their rivals could.
sample_answers.c: British possessions (such as Egypt, South Africa, and Nigeria) form a scattered network centered on strategic ports and the Cape-to-Cairo corridor, while French holdings form a vast contiguous bloc across West and North Africa, reflecting France's ambition for an integrated West African empire.

q3.stimulus: The map shows Africa in 1914 with European colonial possessions marked: British territories (including Egypt, Sudan, South Africa, Rhodesia, Nigeria, Kenya, and the Gold Coast), French territories (a vast bloc across North and West Africa including Algeria, French West Africa, and Madagascar), German colonies (Togoland, Cameroon, German South-West Africa, German East Africa), Belgian Congo, Portuguese Angola and Mozambique, and Italian Libya, Eritrea, and Somaliland. Only Ethiopia and Liberia are independent.
